title: Load group_vars in the CD deploys
description: Every CD deploy (test and production) has failed since b2ab1cf (2026-09-24) at 'Ensure the NodeSource apt repository is present': 'node_major_version' is undefined. The variable lives in infra/ansible/group_vars/all.yml, which Ansible loads only next to an inventory file or playbook. .github/workflows/cd.yml passes the server IP as an inline inventory (-i "IP,") and runs playbooks/deploy.yml, so neither location applies. Local 'just server-*-deploy' recipes use inventory.ini and work. Because the failing task runs after git pull and uv sync but before migrate and the Gunicorn restart, servers end up with new code on disk and an unmigrated database; when Gunicorn restarts (for example after apt upgrade), pages that need new columns return 500. Seen on hci-test /publication/P000006/detail on 2026-10-12. Fix: pass the group vars to both ansible-playbook calls in cd.yml with -e @group_vars/all.yml.
acceptance_criteria:
- Both deploy jobs in cd.yml pass -e @group_vars/all.yml.
- ansible-playbook --syntax-check passes for playbooks/deploy.yml with the same arguments.
- just ci passes.
- After merge, the next CD run gets past the Node.js tasks and runs migrate (checked in the Actions log).
close_reason: cd.yml now passes -e @group_vars/all.yml to both deploys. Reproduced with ansible-playbook and an inline inventory: node_major_version was undefined without it and 26 with it. Still to check after merge: the next CD run gets past Node.js and runs migrate.

title: Create the server .env during init
description:
Server initialization fails at the "Migrate the database" task. The init playbook runs manage.py (migrate, then collectstatic) right after it clones the repo, and manage.py loads its settings from the .env file in the root of the repository. On a fresh server there is no .env yet, so DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE is unset and Django cannot load its settings. Today the only fix is to SSH in, write .env by hand, and rerun init.

Add a task to the init playbook, after the project is installed and before anything runs manage.py, that creates .env from .env.example when the file does not exist. Fill in only the values needed to boot on a server: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.prod, ENV, SUBDOMAIN (from the inventory's subdomain variable), and a newly generated SECRET_KEY, since the production settings refuse to start without one. Leave the other keys empty, so secrets (Clerk, Sentry, backup and other service credentials) are still entered by hand afterward. The task must never overwrite an existing .env, because it holds secrets entered by hand; rerunning init on a set-up server should leave .env untouched. Make the file readable only by the ubuntu user (mode 0600).

Update How to Set Up a Server for the First Time in docs/how-to.md to say init creates .env, and which keys still have to be filled in by hand before the first deploy.
acceptance_criteria:
- On a server with no .env, the init playbook creates one with DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE, ENV, SUBDOMAIN, and a generated SECRET_KEY set, and init runs past migrate and collectstatic.
- Rerunning init on a server that already has a .env leaves the file unchanged (the task reports ok, not changed).
- The created .env has the same keys as .env.example (just env-check would report no differences) and mode 0600.
- just infra-all passes.
- docs/how-to.md describes the new step and the keys left to fill in by hand.

title: Stop CD test deploys from running at the same time
description: cd.yml deploys every pull request whose CI passes to the one test server. Opening a stack of PRs (for example #109-#113 on 2026-10-12) starts one deploy per branch within seconds of each other. They run in parallel against the same checkout and database, so git pull, uv sync, npm install, and migrate can interleave, and the test site ends up on whichever branch finished last. Add a concurrency group to the deploy_to_test job (for example group: deploy-test, cancel-in-progress: true, so only the newest deploy runs) and one to deploy_to_prod (group: deploy-prod, cancel-in-progress: false, so production deploys queue instead of being cancelled).
acceptance_criteria:
- deploy_to_test and deploy_to_prod each have a concurrency group as described.
- just ci passes (the GitHub Actions YAML lint and format checks).
- After merge, opening or updating several PRs at once leaves at most one test deploy running, visible in the Actions tab.
notes: 2026-10-12: Used cancel-in-progress: false for test too, not true as the description suggested. Cancelling a deploy after git pull but before migrate would leave the code ahead of the database, the failure hci-18l fixed. With false, the running deploy finishes and GitHub keeps only the newest pending one, so the test server still ends on the latest branch.
close_reason: Added concurrency groups deploy-test and deploy-prod, both with cancel-in-progress: false (see notes). Still to check after merge: several PRs at once leave at most one test deploy running.

title: Public HLArepo site (#87)
description: Make HLArepo a public, self-contained part of the HCI site at /repo/: browsable without a login, with its own layout, landing page, info pages, and downloads. GitHub #87 asks for a repo with nothing that triggers a login. Repo page content (evidence summary, Mondo and CAR linkouts) was done separately in hci-ss2.7 and is out of scope here. A REST API (Django Ninja) comes later in its own epic.
design:
Problem: the repo views in src/repo/views.py are already public (none use ProtectedViewMixin or protected_view), but the repo templates extend layouts/base.html, whose navbar has a Log In button and dropdowns linking to protected list and create views. The shared evidence partial links every evidence ID to evidence-detail (protected). Breadcrumbs start at home. The footer links to the HCI info pages. So a visitor who clicks almost anything lands on the Clerk sign-in page.

Decisions (maintainer, 2026-10-13):
- Same site. HLArepo stays at /repo/ on the HCI host. A separate hostname was considered and rejected; hci-0m0.1 records it.
- Public layout. Repo pages use their own layout, not layouts/base.html: no HCI navbar, no account activation notice. A Bulma navbar with the HLArepo brand on the left and only a small, unobtrusive link back to the HCI in the upper-right corner. Rule for every public page: link only to repo-* URLs, static files, external sites, or the HCI home page (public). A test that fetches every internal link as an anonymous user enforces this.
- Footer. Same logos (ClinGen, Stanford Medicine), funding text, source link, and Git SHA as the HCI footer, but the text says HLArepo and the info links go to repo pages (/repo/about, /repo/contact, /repo/citing, /repo/help, /repo/acknowledgements, /repo/collaborators). Share the logo and funding markup between the two footers so they don't drift.
- Info pages. HLArepo versions of the six core pages, with text adapted from the HCI pages (same contact email, citation URL https://hci.clinicalgenome.org/repo/). The maintainer will edit the wording later.
- Landing page. The repo search page (repo-search, /repo/) becomes the landing page: a title and subtitle like the HCI home page, the HCI logo (static/hci/img/hci-logo.png), a short description of HLArepo, a downloads section, then the search table.
- Ordering. Published curations are listed by published_at, newest first. The table shows a Published date instead of Updated.
- Type column. Dropped from the repo table and from CurationTable (curation search and HCI home); allele vs haplotype is obvious from which column is filled.
- Downloads. JSON (existing, full nested data), CSV, and XLSX. CSV is one file, one row per published curation, no zip: a haplotype is represented by its name alone (the name already encodes its alleles, e.g. DRB1*15:01~DQB1*06:02), and the evidence summary is a quoted text column, which Excel, pandas, and R read fine. XLSX has two sheets: Curations (same columns as the CSV) and Evidence (one row per evidence record, keyed by curation ID). CSV and XLSX share one flat-row builder in src/repo/serializers.py built from PUBLIC_CURATION_FIELDS and PUBLIC_EVIDENCE_FIELDS, so the public field lists stay the single source of truth.
- Copy and Recurate stays on the repo detail page behind its can_curate check; on the same site there is no reason to move it.
- Curator identities on public pages are an open question (hci-0m0.2); hci-0m0.4 applies the answer.
close_reason: HLArepo is a public, self-contained site at /repo/ with its own layout, landing page, info pages, and JSON/CSV/XLSX downloads, and hides curator identities.

title: Add restore.yml playbook, just recipes, and revert runbook
description: Add the restore playbook, recipes, and runbook. One procedure covers both cases: reverting a bad deploy (restore that deploy's pre-deployment/ backup and check out its 'from' SHA, so code and data go back together) and recovering from corruption (restore a daily/ or pre-deployment/ backup and keep the current code, or check out a given SHA). Create infra/ansible/playbooks/restore.yml taking backup_name (asserted) and optional restore_sha: stop gunicorn.socket and gunicorn.service (new tasks/admin/gunicorn_stop.yml; both must stop, or the socket starts the service again on the next request), take a pre-restore/ backup (tasks/admin/django_dbbackup_prerestore.yml), optionally check out restore_sha then git_sha/uv_sync/npm_install, dbrestore --noinput --uncompress -i (tasks/admin/django_dbrestore.yml), migrate (a no-op when code and backup match), collectstatic, gunicorn_start. If any step after the stop fails, the site stays down on purpose; that's safer than serving code that doesn't match the schema. Add justfile Server-group recipes server-test-restore / server-prod-restore (backup, sha='') and server-prod-list-backups (listbackups over an Ansible ad hoc command). In docs/how-to.md add 'How to Revert a Bad Deploy' (find the backup name in the deploy output or with server-prod-list-backups, restore it with its from-SHA, check that the footer git SHA shows the from-SHA, then open and merge a PR with git revert of the bad commit; until then merge nothing else, or the next deploy puts the bad code back; post-deploy data is in the pre-restore/ backup) and 'How to Restore After Data Corruption' (pick the newest daily/ backup from before the damage; omit the SHA if current code matches, since migrate brings the schema up; mention reverse migrations when only the schema was damaged, and how to recover by hand if the playbook leaves the site down). Losing data entered after the deploy is acceptable (hci-l0k.4); say so plainly, and point to the pre-restore/ backup for copying anything back by hand.
acceptance_criteria: Ansible checks pass; both procedures are rehearsed on the test server (revert a test deploy end to end) and the result noted in this bead; docs/how-to.md updated; just ci passes.
notes:
hci-6qs (removing continuous deployment) changes where the deploy output lives and how the follow-up git revert gets deployed. Keep the runbook wording in line with it.

2026-10-14: The user confirmed that restoring is command-line only, through this playbook and its just recipes. There is no restore button in the admin; see the epic's design.
From hci-l0k.7: the default SqliteBackupConnector restores by writing the backup over the file at DATABASES NAME. Stop Gunicorn first, as planned, and check there's no leftover hci.db-journal or hci.db-wal file. SQLite would apply a stale one to the restored file and corrupt it.
From hci-l0k.13: the admin's Back up now button writes manual/{subdomain}-{username}-{UTC timestamp}.sqlite3.gz. The runbook should list manual/ next to daily/ and pre-deployment/ when choosing a backup. hci-l0k.13 left the docs/how-to.md mention to this bead, because the runbook doesn't exist yet.

title: Database backup, restore, and deploy revert
description: Back up the production database and make a bad deploy revertible. Prod stores everything in one SQLite file, src/hci.db, on the local disk of a single Lightsail instance, and there are no backups at all. No models have FileField or ImageField, so the database is the only data to protect. Goals: an automatic backup before every deploy, so code and data can be reverted to exactly where they were; a daily backup at midnight Pacific, for damage found long after a deploy; a "Back up now" button in the admin for superusers; backups stored off the server in S3; an automated weekly check that backups restore; and a rehearsed runbook plus Ansible playbook for reverting a deploy or restoring a backup.
design:
Risks. Every deploy runs manage.py migrate against the live database, so a bad migration or buggy code can damage data with no way back. The instance can also be lost, or a bug can quietly corrupt data over days.

Tool. django-dbbackup with S3 storage through django-storages. Its default SqliteBackupConnector uses SQLite's online backup API, which takes a consistent copy while Gunicorn is serving. A plain cp does not promise that. Restoring writes over hci.db, so the app must be stopped during a restore. Backups are gzip-compressed.

Storage. One private S3 bucket per Terraform workspace (test, prod): public access blocked, SSE, and a 90-day expiry rule. No versioning, since every backup name is unique. Four key prefixes, so the right backup is easy to find in an incident: pre-deployment/ (deploy playbook, before migrate), daily/ (daily timer), manual/ (the admin's "Back up now" button), and pre-restore/ (restore playbook, just before it overwrites the database, so a restore can itself be undone).

Credentials. Lightsail instances can't have IAM instance roles, so each server uses an IAM user limited to list/get/put/delete on its own bucket. Its keys live in the server's .env, which is kept by hand and not managed by Ansible. A second, read-only IAM user on the prod bucket is used by the weekly restore check in GitHub Actions.

Naming. Pre-deployment backups are named with both SHAs, for example pre-deployment/hci-3f2a9c1-to-88c5e47-2026-09-25T180102Z.sqlite3.gz. The backup holds the data exactly as the old code left it, and the "from" SHA says which code matches it. That pairing is what a revert needs.

Ansible constraints. init.yml can't be re-run on a live server (it runs loaddata and caddy start), so anything existing servers need must also be placed from deploy.yml, using tasks that are safe to re-run. Follow the existing layout: tasks/install/, tasks/placement/, tasks/admin/. infra/ has no READMEs and isn't in docs.json, so document infra changes in docs/how-to.md.

Ordering. The beads are ordered so each one can be deployed and leaves prod working.

Schedule. The daily backup runs at midnight Pacific (00:00 America/Los_Angeles). systemd follows daylight saving time, so that's 07:00 or 08:00 UTC. The user chose this on 2026-10-14. The user confirmed 90-day retention on 2026-10-14. A failed daily backup alerts by email through Amazon SES (hci-l0k.3).

Admin panel. Superusers get a "Back up now" button in the Django admin. The admin doesn't list, download, or restore backups. A restore can't run from the admin: users and sessions live in the database, so the admin can't load without one, and a restore has to stop Gunicorn first. Restoring is command-line only (hci-l0k.11). The user chose this on 2026-10-14.

Rejected alternatives:
- Lightsail automatic snapshots only. Cheap and cover the whole machine, but can't be taken on demand before each deploy without extra AWS tooling, can't restore just the database without building a new instance, and are kept only 7 days. A complement, not a replacement (hci-l0k.5).
- Plain sqlite3 .backup plus aws s3 cp in a shell script. No new dependencies, but django-dbbackup gives naming, compression, restore, and listbackups as management commands, and keeps working if we leave SQLite.
- Litestream. Point-in-time restore is more than a low-traffic curation tool needs, and it adds a daemon to run and watch. Revisit if losing up to a day of work is too much.
- Reverse migrations instead of restoring. Keeps post-deploy data, but only works when every migration reverses and the bug didn't damage data. The runbook mentions it as an option when only the schema is damaged.
- git revert on main as the only code rollback. The site would run new code on the old schema until CI and CD finish, and the revert must pass CI mid-incident. The restore playbook changes code and data together while the app is stopped. The git revert still has to happen afterward, but nothing waits on it.
- Restore check on the test server. Test runs whatever branch was deployed last, so migrate --check fails when test has migrations prod doesn't, which mixes up "bad backup" with "schemas out of sync". It would also put prod data (user emails and PHI-agreement data) on the test server.

title: Decide: read secrets from Secrets Manager at deploy time or run time?
description:
Moving the server's secrets to AWS Secrets Manager needs one decision first: where do the secrets get read?

Option 1 (recommended): at deploy time. Ansible runs on the developer's machine with that developer's AWS profile, reads the workspace's secret from Secrets Manager, and writes the server's .env (mode 0600). The server never needs AWS credentials to read secrets, and the app keeps reading .env as it does now. The trade-off: changing a secret takes a deploy (or rerunning the task that writes .env) before the app sees it.

Option 2: at run time. Django's settings fetch the secret from Secrets Manager with boto3 when the app starts. A secret change takes only a restart. The trade-off: Lightsail instances can't use IAM instance profiles, so the server needs a long-lived IAM access key in .env just to read the other secrets, which leaves a secret on disk anyway and adds an AWS call to every startup, including manage.py commands.

Which option should we use? Answer by closing this bead with the choice as the close reason.

title: Send email through Amazon SES
description: Let the app send email, starting with alerts when the nightly database backup fails (hci-l0k.9), and later for anything else that needs it, such as notifying curators. The app sends no email today: there are no EMAIL_* settings, and alerting goes through Sentry and UptimeRobot. Goals: a verified SES sending identity per environment, credentials on each server, Django configured to send through SES, and a way to check that it works.
design:
Identity. One SES domain identity per Terraform workspace on the server's own subdomain: hci.clinicalgenome.org (prod) and hci-test.clinicalgenome.org (test), created on the aws.stanford-clingen-projects provider in us-west-2. Easy DKIM's three CNAME records go into the clinicalgenome.org zone through the aws.route-53 provider, like subdomain.tf. A per-subdomain identity keeps the HCI from sending as all of clinicalgenome.org, and DKIM on the subdomain aligns with the organizational domain under relaxed DMARC.

Transport. Django's built-in SMTP backend against email-smtp.us-west-2.amazonaws.com on port 587 with STARTTLS. No new dependency. django-ses was rejected because it adds a package for no gain at this volume. SMTP credentials come from an IAM user per workspace allowed only ses:SendRawEmail on its identity; Terraform derives the SMTP password from the access key (ses_smtp_password_v4). The secret lands in Terraform state, which is kept encrypted in the stanford-infra bucket. The keys go in each server's hand-kept .env, like the backup credentials.

Recipients. Alerts go to a custom ALERT_EMAILS setting (comma-separated env var), not Django's ADMINS. Setting ADMINS turns on Django's default mail_admins handler for every 500 error, which would duplicate Sentry.

Sandbox. New SES accounts start in the sandbox, where mail goes only to verified addresses, at most 200 messages a day. That's enough for backup alerts if each recipient verifies their address. Sending to arbitrary curators later needs a production access request in the AWS console, which is a manual step for the user.

Dev and test. Dev uses the console backend and tests use locmem, so neither needs AWS. Only prod settings use SMTP.

title: Remove continuous deployment
description:
.github/workflows/cd.yml deploys automatically. When CI succeeds for a PR, it deploys the PR branch to the test server. When CI succeeds for a push to main, it deploys main to production. So merging or pushing changes a live server. The project has one maintainer, who already deploys with just sted and just sprd and wants to deploy only on purpose. CD also keeps SSH private keys for both servers in GitHub secrets, so anyone who can change a workflow on a branch that runs with them can reach the servers.

Deploy only with the just recipes, which run infra/ansible/playbooks/deploy.yml from the maintainer's machine. Replace what CD gave for free (hci-6qs.1, hci-6qs.2), then delete cd.yml (hci-6qs.3).
design:
What CD provided, and its replacement:
- CI gate. CD deployed only after CI passed. The recipes use gh to check that the latest CI run for the commit being deployed succeeded.
- The playbook matches the deployed code. CD ran the playbook from the commit it deployed. A local deploy runs the local playbook while the server pulls the branch from GitHub, so an uncommitted or unpushed playbook change could ship with code that doesn't match it. The recipes refuse a dirty tree, or a local commit that differs from the remote branch the server will pull.
- Deploy history. The Actions history recorded what was deployed and when. The playbook now appends a line to a log on the server. src/version.txt still records the current SHA.

Decisions:

title: Make the Ansible init playbook safe to rerun on a live server
description:
Rerunning infra/ansible/playbooks/init.yml (just stei / just spri) on an existing server isn't safe. Found while fixing the missing-npm deploy failure (Node was only installed by init.yml; now deploy.yml includes tasks/install/node.yml too).

Problems:
1. It runs migrate but gunicorn_start.yml only ensures gunicorn is started, so the old code keeps serving against the new schema.
2. tasks/admin/caddy_start.yml runs 'caddy start', which likely fails when Caddy is already running.
3. django_loaddata.yml reloads curation/fixtures/demographics.json on every run, overwriting those rows by pk.
4. The Gunicorn unit files, the Caddyfile, and the fail2ban config are placed with no daemon-reload, restart, or reload, so changes don't take effect.
5. install/project.yml's npm ci has creates: node_modules, so it's skipped if Bun left a node_modules.

Plan:
- Caddy: use the systemd caddy service (enabled, started) with a reload handler on Caddyfile changes. First check how Caddy runs now on each server (systemctl status caddy; pgrep -a caddy). If it was started with 'caddy start', it needs a one-time 'caddy stop'. Doing that is a manual step for the user.
- Gunicorn: add handlers that run daemon-reload and restart on unit file changes, and restart after migrate.
- fail2ban: add a reload handler on config changes.
- loaddata: run only when the demographic table is empty.
- Move the shared steps (Node, uv, project deps, migrate, collectstatic, restart) into task files that both init.yml and deploy.yml include, so the two can't drift apart.
The agent must not run playbooks against the servers; the user does that.

title: Match legacy users by verified secondary email on first Clerk login
description:
On a user's first Clerk login, Stage 2 of ClerkBackend.authenticate (src/auth_/backends.py) links the Clerk account to a legacy HCI user by matching User.username. It checks only the primary email, with an exact, case-sensitive match, because the callback view (src/auth_/views.py) passes only the primary as clerk_email.

Example: legacy user bar@site.org signs in with a Clerk account whose primary email is foo@site.org and whose secondary is bar@site.org. Stages 1 and 2 miss, and Stage 3 creates an empty foo@site.org user. The old account keeps its curations, reviews, and PHI flags but is never linked. Every later login matches the new account in Stage 1, so an admin has to fix it by hand. A stored Foo@site.org fails against a Clerk foo@site.org in the same way. Only first logins are affected. Once a profile has a clerk_user_id, Stage 1 matches it whatever the emails are.

Fix: in callback, collect the verified secondary emails and pass them to authenticate() as a new clerk_secondary_emails kwarg (a list of strings, default empty). Log how many were found, but not the addresses. In Stage 2, try the primary, then the secondaries, using username__iexact. When a secondary matches, log that. Consider a small private helper for the lookup. The rules are in design.
design:
Decisions:
- Only verified secondary emails count. Clerk lets a user add an address before verifying it. If unverified addresses counted, anyone could add another person's email to their Clerk account and take over that person's HCI account on first login. An address is verified when email.verification is non-null and its status == "verified". In clerk_backend_api, verification can be null, and the status enums are str subclasses, so comparing to the string works. Skip the entry whose id is primary_email_address_id. The primary email keeps its current behavior.
- The primary email wins. If it matches a user, use that user, even if a secondary matches someone else.
- Refuse to guess. If the primary misses and the verified secondaries match more than one distinct user, log an error naming the Clerk user ID and the matching usernames, and return None. Do the same when one iexact lookup matches several users (e.g. both Foo@site.org and foo@site.org exist). The callback already redirects to login on None, and an admin resolves the conflict.
- Stage 3 doesn't change. A new user still gets the primary email as both username and email.
- Keep the clerk_email kwarg and add clerk_secondary_emails, so existing callers and tests keep working.
acceptance_criteria: Write tests first in src/auth_/tests.py. ClerkBackendTest: a secondary email matches and links an existing user; the primary beats a secondary when they match different users; matching is case-insensitive for primary and secondary; secondaries matching two users return None, log an error, and create or link nothing; an iexact lookup matching two users returns None; the no-match path still creates a user from the primary. CallbackViewTest: _make_clerk_user supports extra emails with a verification status; verified secondaries are passed to authenticate(); unverified and verification=None emails aren't; end to end, a legacy user matched by a verified secondary is logged in. The authenticate docstring describes the new Stage 2. The src/auth_/README.md entries for backends.py, views.py, and tests.py are updated. just ci passes.

title: Improve evidence demographics
description:
The only note was "HCI: Improve demographics", with no detail. The intent must be confirmed (hci-z8m.1) before any code changes.

Current state: Demographic (src/curation/models.py) has one field, group (max_length=20, unique). Groups come from src/curation/fixtures/demographics.json, which holds seven Huddart et al. 2019 biogeographic groups: American, East Asian, European, Central/South Asian, Near Eastern, Oceanian, and Sub-Saharan African. The fixture is loaded by hand. Evidence has a demographics M2M (through table evidence_demographic_map), demographics_text_quotes (added in 9c2ae76 for GitHub #78), and demographics_notes. EvidenceEditForm.clean() requires groups when typing_method is imputation, and requires quotes whenever groups are selected. serialize_evidence publishes group names only. Demographics don't feed scoring.
design:
Pain points visible in the code:
1. Structure is coarse. Curators can say which groups a study included, but not how many participants, cases, or controls came from each. The #78 thread calls the text-quotes field a stopgap "until we have a more structured way to capture the data." For the same reason, 88ce6df removed text quotes from the public serializer at the #78 reporter's request.
2. The group list may be incomplete. Huddart et al. 2019 (the PharmGKB groups) also defines admixed groups, such as African American/Afro-Caribbean and Latino, that aren't in the fixture. Verify against the paper. "African American/Afro-Caribbean" wouldn't fit in max_length=20.
3. #78 asked for the quotes field to be "the first field right under the header," but edit.html renders it after the group select.
4. The two clean() rules chain together, and neither help_text mentions them, so curators learn them one error at a time.
5. Adding a group needs a fixture edit plus loaddata, or the Django admin.

Candidate options:
A. Quick wins (hci-z8m.2).
B. Complete the Huddart group list: add the missing groups to the fixture plus a data migration so existing deployments get them, and raise Demographic.group max_length (schema migration).
C. Structured per-group demographics (hci-z8m.3). This is the largest option and probably what #78 meant by "a more structured way."
D. After C, decide whether the structured data (and possibly the quotes) is public in src/repo/serializers.py and the repo templates.

A is small and independent. B and C each change the schema and should each be one reviewable change with migrations. D depends on C. B and D fold into hci-z8m.3 unless the decision splits them out.

title: Validate duplicate HLA-disease pairs on curation creation
description: GitHub #77. Nothing stops a curator from creating a second or third curation for an allele/haplotype + disease pair that is already being curated. CurationCreateForm has no clean(), and Curation has no uniqueness constraint. In #77 a curator accidentally created a duplicate T1DM / DRB1*03:01 pair on the test site. Requested behavior: if one curation already exists for the pair, alert the curator with its C-number and whether it is risk or protective, and allow a second after confirmation. If two exist, block a third. Two are allowed because the working group allows one curation for risk evidence and one for protective evidence.
design:
Validate in CurationCreateForm.clean(). It is the only path for curators to start a new, independent curation, and it leaves curation_copy untouched. curation_copy (copy and recurate) calls Curation.objects.create directly with the same allele/haplotype and disease and copied_from set to the published source. A copy is a new version of an existing curation, not a new line of curation, so copies are never blocked and don't count as a separate pair. Count only root curations (copied_from__isnull=True), so a published curation and its copies count as one pair.

Matching by foreign key is equivalent to matching CAR ID, haplotype name, and Mondo ID, because Allele.car_id, Haplotype.name, and Disease.mondo_id are unique. It also works for alleles whose car_id is null.

There is no curation-level direction yet. 'Protective' exists only as the per-evidence Evidence.is_protective, and a new curation has no evidence. So showing or enforcing risk vs. protective waits on a decision (hci-8d9.2).

Rejected alternatives:
- Live HTMX lookup when the selects change. Nicer UX, but it adds an endpoint, a partial, and JS wiring. Confirm-on-submit gives the same protection with less code, and the live lookup can be added later on top of the same query helper.
- A database UniqueConstraint on (allele, disease, direction) conditioned on copied_from IS NULL. It needs a curation-level direction field and still needs the form check for a friendly message. Revisit after hci-8d9.2.
- Creating the curation and then showing messages.warning. The duplicate already exists by then, which is what #77 wants to avoid.

title: Import curations from a normalized file
description: Add an internal-only import_curations management command in the curation app. It reads a normalized file of curations and evidence, cleans dirty spreadsheet values, finds or creates the supporting alleles, haplotypes, diseases, and publications, validates evidence the same way the edit view does, supports --dry-run, reports errors by source row, is idempotent via a new Curation.import_key, and attributes records to a --user. GitHub #63.
design:
Problem: every curation is entered by hand, one form at a time. The main source of existing curations is the concordance spreadsheets curators filled out before the HCI existed, and re-keying them is slow and error prone. The spreadsheets are dirty: '4' vs '4-field' for resolution, allele names with or without HLA- and with stray spaces (DRB1 *03:01), yes/no as Y, yes, TRUE, or x, and typing methods as free text instead of the HCI's codes. The spreadsheets are not in the repo.

Shape: a management command run by a developer on the server or locally (uv run manage.py import_curations path --user ...). No web UI. Three stages. Read turns the file into plain row objects and is isolated behind one function, so the format decision only touches the reader. Normalize is a set of small pure functions, one per concept. A value that can't be mapped is an error on that row, never a guess. New synonyms are a one-line change. Validate and write finds or creates supporting records by natural key (allele name, mondo_id, pubmed_id), using the same clients as the create views to fill in CAR ID, disease name, and publication metadata. Evidence is validated through EvidenceEditForm plus the curation.validators.views helpers, so imports pass exactly the checks a curator's input does, and new validation applies to imports for free.

All or nothing: everything runs in one transaction. --dry-run does all the work and rolls back. A real run commits only if every row is valid, so the database is never half-imported. External lookups can't be rolled back, but they are read-only. The report lists, per source row, create vs reuse for each supporting record, create vs 'already imported' for the curation, and any errors, then totals.

Attribution: added_by is the --user. History records get _history_user = user and _change_reason 'Imported from <file name>' (simple-history reads both off the instance before saving). Status: IN_PROGRESS curations with needs_review=True evidence, so a curator reviews every item before submitting through the normal workflow (Curation.can_submit).

Rejected alternatives. Django fixtures: they need stored codes, primary keys, FK pks, and slugs up front, so the cleaning script would be most of this work anyway. loaddata saves in raw mode, which skips our save() overrides (slugs like C000123 never get generated), clean(), and form validation. It has no dry run and can't look up an existing allele by name. Moving data between HCI databases is the backup and restore epic's job (hci-l0k). A web upload page: adds an upload surface, long-running requests (external API calls per new record), and report UI, for what is a rare migration. If imports become routine, a view can call the importer's core function later. Reading the raw .xlsx files with per-spreadsheet column maps: couples the HCI to files we don't control. Better to convert each spreadsheet once to one normalized format and let normalization handle cell-level mess.

Note: publications are PubMed-only now (preprints were removed), so there is no DOI or rxiv path.

title: Production logging: journald, retention, and easy access
description: Give production logging a deliberate design. Today Django logs go both to a size-rotated logs/hci.log and to stderr, which lands in journald unconfigured; Caddy writes a JSON access log with default rolling; Sentry catches errors; nothing leaves the server, and reading logs means SSHing in and knowing three places to look. Goals: one obvious place to read app logs, rotation and retention chosen on purpose and shared by every process, no files created as a side effect of loading settings, and a short documented way to read logs.
design:
Current state (before this epic):
- src/config/settings/prod.py sends the root logger at INFO to a RotatingFileHandler (logs/hci.log in the repo root, 5 MB x 5 backups, about 30 MB max, verbose format) and to a stderr StreamHandler (simple format: level and message only).
- prod.py creates logs/ and touches hci.log at import. That runs everywhere prod settings load, including migrate and collectstatic during deploys and the ci.yml and codecov.yml jobs that set DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.prod.
- Rotation is size-only, so history could be months or hours. RotatingFileHandler assumes one writer, but deploy-time management commands (and the daily backup timer, hci-l0k.9) write the same file, so lines near a rotation can be lost or misfiled.
- Gunicorn runs as a systemd unit, so its stderr already goes to the journal. Every Django line is stored twice. Gunicorn's own messages go only to the journal. journald uses Ubuntu 24.04 defaults: persistent, capped at 10% of disk (max 4 GB), no time limit.
- Caddy writes JSON access logs to /var/log/caddy/access.log, which fail2ban reads (jail.d/caddy.conf, caddy-blocked filter). Rolling uses Caddy defaults (100 MB, 10 files, 90 days). Caddy is started with 'caddy start', not the packaged caddy.service, so it's unclear where its runtime logs go or whether the packaged unit also runs.
- Sentry uses its default Django and logging integrations: ERROR records and unhandled exceptions become events, INFO becomes breadcrumbs. Whether alerts notify anyone depends on Sentry alert rules we can't see from the repo.
- Logs hold personal data (auth_/backends.py logs curator emails when linking Clerk accounts), so retention must be chosen on purpose.

Decisions:
- journald is the single sink for app logs (pending hci-y0x.1). journald adds time, host, unit, and PID, so the console format is only level, logger name, and message. It handles multiple writers, rotation, and retention, and journalctl filters by time, unit, and priority.
- 90-day retention everywhere (pending hci-y0x.2). It matches backup retention and the Caddy default: long enough for problems reported weeks later, short enough not to keep personal data forever.
- Caddy's access log stays a JSON file, not journald, because fail2ban's filter expects that format and path.
- Sentry stays the alerting layer. No new alerting tool.
- Gunicorn's access log stays off. Caddy already records every request with more detail (client IP, TLS, timing).

Rejected alternatives:
- Keep the file and fix rotation (WatchedFileHandler plus logrotate, daily, 90 rotations). Time-based and multi-process safe, but still stores every line twice, adds a logrotate config, and leaves two places to look. Only worth it if someone needs plain files for another tool.
- Structured JSON app logs (for example python-json-logger). Pays off only once logs go to a system that indexes fields. With journald and grep, plain text is easier. Revisit with hci-y0x.3.

title: Decide: is losing post-deploy data on revert acceptable?
description:
Is it acceptable that reverting a bad deploy loses data entered since that deploy?

Restoring a pre-deployment backup drops every change made after the deploy. The working assumption is yes for this low-traffic tool: the restore playbook takes a pre-restore/ backup first, so lost data can be copied back by hand if someone needs it. Reverse migrations (migrate <app> <previous_migration> plus a code rollback) keep post-deploy data, but only work when every migration reverses and the bug didn't damage data. The runbook will mention them as an option when only the schema is damaged. The answer decides the runbook wording in hci-l0k.11.

title: Decide: GPG-encrypt database backups client-side?
description:
Should database backups be GPG-encrypted client-side?

Context: the backup bucket uses S3 server-side encryption, and only the server's writer IAM user and the prod read-only IAM user can read it. The database holds curator emails and data covered by the PHI agreement (see docs/design.md). django-dbbackup can GPG-encrypt backups with --encrypt. The cost is a GPG key that must be kept safe and made available on both servers (to restore) and in GitHub Actions (for the weekly restore check).

If yes: hci-l0k.7 adds the DBBACKUP_GPG_RECIPIENT settings, and the backup and restore commands in hci-l0k.8, hci-l0k.9, hci-l0k.10, and hci-l0k.11 need --encrypt/--decrypt, plus key distribution. If no: SSE plus tight IAM is the protection.

title: EP review follow-up
description:
Follow-up to the expert panel (EP) review workflow, which shipped in commit 6bc9d88 (fork renamed to 'copy and recurate' in cec04de). The panel has used the workflow and sent feedback, and GitHub #58, #62, and #85 still have loose ends. What's left:

- Status names don't match how the panel talks. To the panel, 'provisional' means 'finished by the curator and waiting for us.' So today's Ready for Review becomes Provisional, and today's Provisional becomes Approved.
- There is no EP review date. added_at, updated_at, and history record when someone clicked a button in the HCI. The panel wants the date it actually met, which can be days or weeks earlier.
- An override isn't recorded. Picking an ep_classification that differs from the suggestion only triggers a JS confirm(). #62 asks that an override require a note, kept in its own field.
- EP notes are hard to find on the curation detail page. They show only when ep_classification is set, so feedback on a send-back (the normal case) is invisible to the curator.
- The public repo page shows too little: no evidence summary (#85), no Mondo or CAR links. (Done in hci-ss2.7.)
- Curators can't tell which form fields become public in HLArepo and the JSON export.
- A score of 0 shows as '------'. #62 asks for 'No Classification Set.'
- Confirmations use window.confirm (#58 asks for a Bulma modal). Publish is a plain link, so a GET publishes, and any prefetcher or crawler could publish a curation.

Goal: the workflow uses the panel's vocabulary and records what the panel decided, when, and why. The public record shows the parts that matter.

Source: user notes 'HCI: Work on EP review feedback.'
design:
Status rename uses new codes, not just new labels. RFR (Ready for Review) becomes PRV (Provisional), and PRO (Provisional) becomes APR (Approved). Neither PRV nor APR has ever been stored, so the data migration is order-independent and PRO stops meaning anything. Rejected: relabel only and keep RFR/PRO, because PRO would mean Approved while the constant, code, and old exports say Provisional. Rejected: reuse PRO for the new Provisional, because the migration would have to run PRO->APR strictly before RFR->PRO, and old history rows and downloaded JSON would silently change meaning.

Classification override: ep_classification stays the single authoritative classification. The new field holds the reason (ep_override_reason), and Curation.is_classification_overridden gives templates and serializers the flag. Rejected: a separate ep_override_classification column, which would leave two classification fields every reader must reconcile. The reason is what the panel actually asked to capture.

The EP review date is the date the panel met, entered by the reviewer. The date the HCI recorded the approval still comes from django-simple-history, as the original design chose over dedicated timestamp columns.

Public vs internal fields (decided in hci-ss2.8): public are the evidence summary, EP classification, panel, EP review date, ep_additional_notes, and ep_override_reason, plus most evidence data. Internal are needs_review and every *_notes field on Evidence.

Public-field badge uses a title attribute plus is-sr-only text, since Bulma has no tooltip component. title doesn't show on touch or keyboard focus. Switch to a CSS tooltip in custom.css later if the panel finds it too subtle.

Split with GitHub #87 (public repo site): #87 owns access control, routing, and hosting of the repo pages. This epic owns what those pages show. Both touch repo/templates/repo/detail.html, so whichever lands second rebases. The internal links the reused partials render on the repo page (View History to curation-history, evidence rows to evidence-detail) belong to #87.
notes:
Unanswered questions (none block this epic):
1. Does 'standardized' in #85 ('Standardized Evidence Summary Text') mean templated text? We treat it as free text from the reviewer. If the panel wants a generated starting template (for example, 'HLA-X has a {class} association with {disease} based on N studies...'), that's a follow-up that pre-fills ep_evidence_summary on the review form.
2. Should the repo page credit the reviewer? The HCI user who recorded the review isn't a field; only history has it. Not shown for now.
close_reason: All children closed. The two non-blocking open questions from the epic notes were filed as standalone decision beads.

title: Audit and standardize color usage across the interface
description:

Audit every use of Bulma color modifiers (is-info, is-success, is-warning, is-danger, is-link, is-primary, is-light, has-text-*) in src/**/templates and src/**/tables.py, then agree on a meaning for each color, write it down in docs/design.md, and apply it.

Known examples as of 2026-09-29:
- Yellow (is-warning) means In Progress (tag), Not Provided (tag), the Provisional banner on the curation detail page, the Review button, the Sent Back for Revision panel, and the demo-site banner.
- Red (is-danger) means both Provisional (status tag) and Needs Review (evidence tag). Provisional was picked red only to tell it apart from yellow In Progress.
- Green (is-success) means Done, Provided, Approved, the Approved banner, and the Publish button.
- Blue (is-info) means Published (tag and banner), and has-text-info colors the public-field badge. published.html passes "is-info is-light" and _generic.html adds is-light again.
- Buttons mix is-link, is-warning, and is-success with no stated rule.
- The EP feedback panel is now a neutral Bulma message (the user found blue strange there).

Check both light and dark themes (base.html sets data-theme="light"), and color contrast for accessibility.

notes: Decided 2026-09-29 (user): one meaning per color. Grey (no modifier) = not finished or neutral (In Progress, Not Provided, Suggested, EP feedback). Yellow = waiting on someone else, or caution (Provisional tag and banner, superseded note, demo banner, 4xx pages). Red = needs fixing (Needs Review, form errors, 500, error messages, EP feedback when sent back). Green = done or approved (Done, Provided, Approved tag and banner, evidence points). Info blue = published or public (Published tag and banner, public-field badge, 'update of' note). Link blue = clickable: every button, including Review and Publish; Cancel is the light variant.

title: Pre-fill the evidence summary with the HCT summary template (#85)
description: GitHub #85 asks for standardized evidence summary text. The HLA Curation Taskforce has a summary template (in this bead's design). Pre-fill ep_evidence_summary on the EP review form from it when the field is empty, so the reviewer starts from the standard structure instead of a blank box. How much the HCI fills in automatically is decided in the blocking decision bead. Likely home: a function in src/curation (for example curation/summary.py) that builds the text from a Curation, called by curation_review for the initial value.
design:
The HCT summary template, verbatim. Its placeholder syntax is the author's own, not a standard format: [text] marks a placeholder or instruction, [If applicable: ...] marks an optional clause, and "[A] OR [B]" marks alternatives.

[Allele/haplotype]–[Disease] Curation Summary
[Allele/haplotype] in [gene(s); write out gene name and introduce the symbol abbreviation] was first reported in association with [disease] by [Author] et al. [year] (PMID: [ ]). [If applicable: In case of haplotype, discuss structure]. [Disease] (MONDO:[ID]) is characterized by [one to three sentences on the core clinical phenotype, with citations]. [If applicable: Phenotypes in the included studies were mapped to MONDO:[ID]. However, [describe the problem, e.g., the studies used different diagnostic criteria or reported a broader/narrower phenotype or subtype than the MONDO term] (PMIDs: [ ]). [Discuss if increased risk or protective association] [If applicable: Sentence if a specific disease phenotype contributed to the total score.]
The classification of the [allele/haplotype]–[disease] pair is based on evidence from [n] publications (PMIDs: [ ]). These were identified through a structured PubMed search and discussed within the ClinGen HLA Curation Taskforce (HCT). The evidence comprises [n] genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and [n] case-control studies. [The allele was heterozygous (monoallelic) in [n]/[N] of the scored evidence and homozygous in [n].] OR [The allele was heterozygous (monoallelic) in all studies.] All evidence was typed at 2-field resolution [, except for [n] studies where the genotyping method allowed 3-field [4-field] resolution]. [All / [n] of [N]] scored associations were statistically significant. [If applicable: In case, non-significant results are included, briefly discuss potential reasons for disagreement.] The total score for the [allele/haplotype]–[disease] pair is [x] points.
In summary, there is [classification] evidence supporting the association between [allele/haplotype] and [disease], based on the published HLA curation framework (PMID: [ ]; SOP version [x]). This classification was approved by the ClinGen HLA Curation Taskforce on [Final approval date].

What the HCI already stores, for each placeholder:
- Allele/haplotype name, disease name, and MONDO ID: on the curation.
- Number of publications and their PMIDs: the included evidence's publications.
- GWAS vs case-control counts: Evidence.is_gwas on included evidence.
- Heterozygous/homozygous counts: Evidence.zygosity.
- Resolution (2-, 3-, or 4-field): Evidence.num_fields.
- How many scored associations were significant: Evidence.has_association.
- Total score: Curation.score. Classification: ep_classification. Approval date: ep_review_date.
- HCT name: EP_CHOICES.

Not stored, so a person has to write them: the gene's full name, the first report (author, year, PMID; it may not be among the curated evidence), the clinical phenotype description, haplotype structure, MONDO mapping problems, risk vs protective discussion, the framework PMID, and the SOP version (the last two could become constants).
acceptance_criteria: Tests written first: the pre-filled text for a curation with known evidence matches the expected text; the review form doesn't overwrite an existing ep_evidence_summary. src/curation/README.md updated. just ci passes.

title: Decide: new URL and ID scheme for all entities, including curations
description:
Decide the URL and ID scheme for every entity, including curations. The user's ideas, not yet decided: publications use the PMID as the ID in URLs and display; diseases use the Mondo ID; alleles use something similar (CAR ID or allele name); haplotypes use a key derived from their member alleles; curations get an ID built from the pair being curated (allele or haplotype plus disease) so it says what the curation is about, with a UUID or other suffix because the same pair can be curated more than once (for example a copy made to recurate).

Questions to settle:
1. Allele key: CAR ID (nullable today, so it would have to become required, with a data check first) or the allele name (contains * and :, awkward in URLs)?
2. Haplotype key: haplotypes have no external ID. Is a key built from the member alleles' keys acceptable, and how long can it get?
3. Curation ID format: what does it look like in a URL, for example <allele key>-<Mondo ID>-<suffix>? Is the suffix a full UUID, a short random string, or a per-pair counter? Is it still readable enough to say out loud or type into an issue, as curators do with C numbers today (#77)?
4. Changing keys: if a curation's ID includes its allele and disease, what happens when a curator changes either before publishing? Is the ID fixed at creation?
5. Evidence IDs: keep E numbers, or a key scoped to the curation?
6. Published curations are already public by C number. Keep their C numbers and use the new scheme only for new curations, or give them new IDs with permanent redirects from old URLs and a JSON version bump?
7. Primary keys: keep integer pks and change only URLs and display (the current approach), or make any external ID the database key? See the epic's design for why the latter was rejected before.
acceptance_criteria: The user has answered. The answers are recorded in this bead's notes and the epic's design is updated to match. hci-iz5.1 through hci-iz5.6 are updated, superseded, or closed to fit, and new beads are filed for any entity the new scheme adds.

title: Move max_length values into constants modules
description: Notes: "HCI: Add max lengths to constants module". Every max_length is a bare literal in a models.py, and some carry explanatory comments. title: Use stable external IDs instead of HCI IDs where possible
description: Speculative. For entities with a reliable external ID, stop showing the HCI ID (the slug, for example D000017) and possibly key URLs by the external ID instead, with permanent redirects from old slug URLs. The user also wants to rethink URLs and IDs for every entity, including curations (hci-iz5.7). Settle that before working hci-iz5.1 through hci-iz5.6, which reflect an older, narrower scope (diseases and publications only). Source: the user's note 'For entities with stable IDs, get rid of HCI IDs'.
design:
Current state. Every major model has a slug (verbose name 'Human-Readable ID') that save() fills in from the pk: Allele A, Haplotype H, Disease D, Publication P, Curation C, Evidence E, for example A000001. External IDs: Allele has car_id (nullable; get_car_id returns None when the Allele Registry has no match) and a unique name like DRB1*15:01. Disease has mondo_id (required, unique, validated to start with MONDO:). Publication has pubmed_id (required, unique; preprints were removed, so there is no DOI). Haplotype, Curation, and Evidence have none. Slugs are used in every detail, history, and change URL, the ID link column in every tables.py, SearchListView search_fields, titles and breadcrumbs, HistoryTable change links, and the public repo JSON (repo/serializers.py exposes slug for allele, haplotype, haplotype alleles, disease, and publication, plus curation_id, evidence_id, and copied_from as HCI IDs). Curators refer to curations by 'C number' in conversation and GitHub issues (#77).

Why. For diseases and publications the HCI ID is a second name nobody outside the HCI recognizes. Curators want MONDO:0005052, not D000017, and know a publication by its PMID.

Recommended approach (for the narrow scope). Keep integer primary keys and the slug columns. Change only the URL key and the displayed label where a reliable external ID exists. Old slug URLs 301 to the new ones so bookmarks and links in issues, emails, and notes keep working. Keeping the slug column costs nothing, keeps simple-history records readable, and is what the redirects look up by. Mondo terms can be obsoleted or merged. The HCI record keeps its old Mondo ID, which is still a stable string. Allele, disease, and publication pages are behind ProtectedViewMixin, and public repo pages link only by curation slug, so public impact is limited to the repo JSON. Templates that pass object.slug to {% url %} should switch to object.get_absolute_url. No data migration is needed.

Rejected. Dropping the slug columns: schema migrations on model and historical tables, breaks the repo JSON, and leaves nothing for redirects to look up. Revisit only after the JSON stops exposing slugs and redirects have been live a while. External ID as primary key: every FK to those tables would change, and fixing a mistyped ID becomes a cascading key change. A display-only change (hci-iz5.3) is the cheapest option, gets most of the visible benefit, and can stand alone.

Side issue: slug is not unique=True on any model, so the database doesn't prevent duplicates, and max_length=7 breaks after 999,999 objects of a type. Neither is urgent, but both show HCI IDs weren't designed as permanent public IDs.

title: Decide: ship logs off the server (Sentry Logs or other)?
description:
Should logs also go off the server, and if so, where?

Recommendation: not now. Start with journald plus Sentry errors, then try Sentry Logs if SSH-based reading turns out to be painful or logs need to survive losing the instance. Options, from least to most setup:
- Sentry Logs: enable_logs=True in sentry_sdk.init, with the logging integration sending INFO or WARNING and above. Uses a vendor and SDK we already have, puts logs next to the errors they explain, no agent. Costs Sentry quota and pricing, and personal data leaves our servers (though send_default_pii=True already sends some).
- AWS CloudWatch Logs through the CloudWatch agent reading journald. Same AWS account, but needs an agent and an IAM user (Lightsail has no instance roles), and docs/design.md already rejected CloudWatch for monitoring as too much overhead.
- A hosted log service (Better Stack, Papertrail, Grafana Cloud Loki) through a journald forwarder. Works well, but a new vendor and account for a small, low-traffic tool.
If logs do go to an indexing system, reconsider structured JSON app logs. Blocks hci-y0x.8 only.
